# The incumbent for Ateles: ad-hoc agent invocation by hand

## Subject

What the ICP (solo technical founder-operator) actually uses today before adopting Ateles: no vendor, no competing platform — direct, unattributed invocation of coding-agent CLIs (claude, similar), coordinated entirely by the operator's own memory and typing.

## Summary

The reader's actual current solution, in their own vocabulary: opening a chat (or several) with claude / Claude Code by hand per task, re-explaining context each session because nothing persists between them, running agents under the operator's own identity with no distinct attribution (a code-writing agent acts as the operator on GitHub with no audit trail tying the signed subject to the action), approving risky actions ad hoc in the chat itself rather than through any declared checkpoint, and accumulating coordination logic as a growing CLAUDE.md plus scattered shell scripts and one-off Python rather than any declared workflow. Failure modes, concretely: (1) zero-context restarts — every session starts from nothing, so the operator re-explains project state, prior decisions, and constraints each time; (2) identity collapse — there is one shared bearer (the operator's own login/keys), so a merge, a payment, or an outbound message done by an agent is indistinguishable after the fact from one done by the operator, and there is no reconstructable record of who authorized what; (3) manual sequencing — running more than one agent means opening multiple chats and hoping they do not conflict, which is bespoke integration work the operator pays for every time a new domain is added; (4) no standing memory — what one session learns is not available to the next, so facts and decisions are re-derived or silently lost; (5) instructions as governance — CLAUDE.md-style prose accretes as the only enforcement mechanism, which is advisory, not binding: nothing fails when it is violated, so it is documentation, not a control.

## Method

Derived from docs/icp.md (origin/main, code-audited ICP) and docs/foundation/charter.md's 'What an operator gets' section (origin/main), which names the ad-hoc baseline explicitly as what the design replaces. Cross-checked against README.md's 'Why this exists' section (origin/main), which lists the same failure modes as the motivating problem.

COMPETITOR TEST RE-RUN 2026-09-21 (first pass): the prior competitor test was invalid — it tested a HYPOTHETICAL competitor ("an orchestration framework with a memory/state add-on could claim to address both") rather than a shipping one, contrary to the /frame-product-argument skill's explicit instruction to "verify any competitor claim against what they ship NOW." Checked against LangGraph's persistence docs (https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence), CrewAI's memory docs (https://docs.crewai.com/en/concepts/memory), and AutoGen's state-management docs/discussions (https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/stable//user-guide/agentchat-user-guide/tutorial/state.html; https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/discussions/6169), confirming AutoGen ships no built-in checkpointing (`save_state()` is manual, developer-serialized; AutoGen has been in maintenance mode since October 2025, checkpointing moved to Microsoft Agent Framework).

COMPETITOR TEST RE-RUN 2026-09-21 (second pass, operator-directed): the first pass argued only reach (thread/process scope). Re-checked against PRIMARY SOURCE CODE, not just doc prose, to test whether LangGraph's Store or CrewAI's entity memory offer typed domain modelling, attribution, or correction semantics that would weaken a kind-of-state distinction: LangGraph's `Item` class read directly from `libs/checkpoint/langgraph/store/base/__init__.py` in langchain-ai/langgraph (via `gh api repos/langchain-ai/langgraph/contents/...`) — confirms `value: dict[str, Any]` (schema-less), no author/attribution field, `updated_at` overwrites with no retained history. CrewAI's `MemoryRecord` read directly from `lib/crewai/src/crewai/memory/types.py` in crewAIInc/crewAI (same method) — confirms a single untyped record shape (`content: str`, `metadata: dict[str, Any]`, `source: str | None` as an origin tag only, no per-field attribution, no versioning), and confirmed via repo directory listing (`gh api repos/crewAIInc/crewAI/contents/lib/crewai/src/crewai/memory`) that no separate `entity_memory.py` exists in the current codebase — the historical short-term/long-term/entity split was collapsed into this one untyped `Memory`/`MemoryRecord` class, consistent with CrewAI's own docs description of a unified memory system. Consolidation-on-duplicate behavior (LLM-arbitrated keep/update/delete, confirmed in `MemoryConfig.consolidation_threshold` docstring) confirms updates overwrite rather than retain superseded values. The discriminator applied, per the operator's framing verified rather than assumed: KIND of state (typed/attributable/correctable record vs. untyped execution/recall state) as primary, with the README's process/horizon distinction (README.md @ origin/main, 'How does this compare to LangGraph / CrewAI / AutoGen?') as a downstream, independently-confirmed consequence rather than the lead argument. Per plan ent_98ef9d45f8a6896fed408f8f decision 'scenarios_must_fail_the_competitor_test', reused rather than reinvented.

COMPETITOR TEST RE-RUN 2026-09-21 (third pass, operator-directed: push vs. pull distinction on MANUAL SEQUENCING): the operator asked whether a key distinction in HOW sequencing works — push vs. pull — un-drops the manual-sequencing failure mode, citing `docs/foundation/work_model.md` (`git -C ~/repos/ateles show origin/main:docs/foundation/work_model.md`, read in full for the sections "Pull is the only delivery; assignment constrains eligibility," "Assignment restricts eligibility; it never creates a lease," "The claim and the lease are one primitive," and "Operator-only tasks are claimed by the operator-facing agent"). Tested against PRIMARY SOURCE CODE for how each framework selects an executor for a step, not documentation prose: CrewAI's `_execute_tasks` method (`lib/crewai/src/crewai/crew.py`, crewAIInc/crewAI, via `gh api repos/crewAIInc/crewAI/contents/...`) — confirms the crew object iterates its task list and calls `task.execute_sync(agent=exec_data.agent, ...)`, resolving and handing off the agent itself; `_create_manager_agent` (same file) confirms the hierarchical process instantiates a manager agent with `allow_delegation=True` for exactly this purpose. LangGraph's `prepare_next_tasks` (`libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_algo.py`, langchain-ai/langgraph, via `gh api repos/langchain-ai/langgraph/contents/...`) — confirms the Pregel scheduler computes the next superstep's tasks unilaterally from graph topology and channel-version bookkeeping (`_triggers`, `trigger_to_nodes`), with dynamic `Send`-based dispatch materialized through an internal constant named `PUSH_TRIGGER`; checked specifically whether the `PULL` task-path tag names an accountable claim (it does not — it names data-flow direction, a node reading its subscribed channels, with no persisted holder read back before the scheduler accepts a task as taken). AutoGen's `SelectorGroupChatManager.select_speaker` (`python/packages/autogen-agentchat/src/autogen_agentchat/teams/_group_chat/_selector_group_chat.py`, microsoft/autogen, via `gh api repos/microsoft/autogen/contents/...`) — confirms the manager selects the next speaker via a ChatCompletion model call, a 1:N inference inside an actor distinct from the executors. No claim/lease primitive (a persisted holder read back after the write) was found in any of the three.

## Conclusion

WHAT ATELES RESOLVES: identity collapse (agents carry AAuth-signed identities distinct from the operator, with every write attributed to the principal it acted for); manual sequencing across domains (one dispatch/claim mechanism rather than per-chat coordination, so adding a domain does not add a second system to run); cross-process, cross-day standing memory as modelled, attributable, correctable RECORD rather than mere recoverable state (Neotoma as one durable, typed, provenance-tracked graph any daemon or runner reads/writes, detailed below); advisory-only governance (declared workflows and gates that mechanically block — a mechanism that does not bind is not a control — rather than prose an agent may or may not follow). WHAT IT DOES NOT RESOLVE: Ateles is a reference architecture you fork and adapt, not an installable product — it does not remove the requirement to read Python, provision keypairs/secrets, and run your own daemons; it does not serve teams or multi-operator organizations (P2-P5 multi-operator authority is designed but unbuilt, per docs/foundation/status.md); it does not offer zero-install onboarding: someone who wants to sign up rather than fork gets no path in.

THE COMPETITOR TEST, RE-RUN AGAINST SHIPPING CAPABILITY (updated 2026-09-21, second pass): each failure mode was checked against what LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen actually ship today (see method for the exact source files/docs read), using the register's own boundary (plan ent_98ef9d45f8a6896fed408f8f decision 'positioning_categories'; restated in README.md's 'How does this compare to LangGraph / CrewAI / AutoGen?': those frameworks orchestrate multi-step LLM calls inside ONE process and coordinate computation; Ateles coordinates long-running background daemons and per-task runners, each with its own signed identity, writing to a canonical record — governed fleets across days, not chains across seconds) as the discriminator, not a feature checklist.

- ZERO-CONTEXT RESTARTS and NO STANDING MEMORY — RESTATED, not borderline, and not primarily on reach. The PRIMARY discriminator is KIND OF STATE, not scope: a checkpointer or memory store persists EXECUTION/RECALL STATE — where a run got to, or a retrievable trace of past interaction — not a MODELLED, TYPED, ATTRIBUTABLE, CORRECTABLE RECORD that is meaningful to a reader who never saw the process that wrote it. Verified directly against source, not assumed: LangGraph's `Item` class (libs/checkpoint/langgraph/store/base/__init__.py, langchain-ai/langgraph) stores `value: dict[str, Any]` — an arbitrary, schema-less, developer-defined blob — plus `key`/`namespace`/`created_at`/`updated_at`. There is no author/attribution field and no supersession semantics: `updated_at` marks the last write, but the prior value is not retained, versioned, or queryable as history. Checkpointer state is stricter still: it is the graph's own developer-defined state object, scoped to and legible only to that graph. CrewAI's `MemoryRecord` (lib/crewai/src/crewai/memory/types.py, crewAIInc/crewAI) confirms the same shape: `content: str` (free text) plus an untyped `metadata: dict[str, Any]`, a `source: str | None` field documented as "for provenance tracking," but this is a single origin tag (e.g. 'user:alice'), not per-field attribution or an audit trail, and there is no separate typed "entity memory" in the current codebase — CrewAI's own docs confirm the earlier short-term/long-term/entity split was collapsed into one untyped `Memory` class. Consolidation on a duplicate is explicitly LLM-arbitrated keep/update/delete (the update path overwrites, it does not retain the superseded value). So: NEITHER framework offers a typed domain-entity model, per-field attribution recording who wrote a value under what authority, or correction semantics that retain a superseded value alongside its replacement. A checkpointer/store fanned out across every process and day would still answer "where did this run get to" or "what does this text vaguely resemble," not "what is true, who said so, and what did it used to be" — which is what Ateles's claim (coordinating legitimate action: who authorized what, against which state) actually requires, since you cannot ask a checkpointer or a memory record who authorized a payment when neither has a concept of "payment," "authorization," or a typed, correctable field for either. The PROCESS/HORIZON argument (thread-scoped vs. cross-process, single-run vs. cross-day) is a real and independently-confirmed consequence of this — LangGraph's own docs say checkpointers are not for cross-process use and route cross-thread needs to Store, and CrewAI's memory is scoped to one crew's local run directory — but it is downstream of the kind-of-state gap, not the primary reason the mode survives: state only the writing run/thread can interpret cannot usefully cross tools regardless of how far you widen its reach, because nothing else could read it as a typed thing. Restated failure mode: "there is no shared, typed, attributable, correctable model of the domain — only untyped execution/recall state scoped to the process or thread that wrote it" — that is what Ateles resolves (Neotoma's entities are typed, versioned via priority-ordered observations, provenance-tracked per field, and correctable in place with both old and new retained) and neither framework ships.

- MANUAL SEQUENCING — RESTATED as a PUSH VS. PULL distinction (operator-directed re-test, 2026-09-21, third pass), not dropped and not borderline. The prior DROP conflated two different questions: whether agents can be sequenced inside a run (they can, and these frameworks do it well) and HOW an executor is selected for a step. Checked against primary source, not documentation prose: CrewAI's own execution loop (`_execute_tasks` in crew.py, crewAIInc/crewAI) iterates `self.tasks` and calls `task.execute_sync(agent=exec_data.agent, ...)` — the crew, a central orchestrating object, resolves and hands each task to an agent object; the agent performs no "is this mine" fitness judgment and holds no lease the crew reads back before assigning. In hierarchical mode this is explicit: `_create_manager_agent` instantiates a manager agent with `allow_delegation=True` whose job is to delegate tasks to the other agents — a push by construction. LangGraph's scheduler (`prepare_next_tasks` in `libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_algo.py`, langchain-ai/langgraph) unilaterally computes, from graph topology and per-node `triggers` against updated channel versions, the set of `PregelTask`s to run next each superstep; a node never chooses to take work, and dynamic dispatch via `Send` is materialized through an internal constant literally named `PUSH_TRIGGER`. (LangGraph's `PULL` task-path tag names the *data-flow direction* — a node reads its input from subscribed channels — not an accountable claim: there is no persisted holder read back before the scheduler accepts a task as taken, checked specifically to rule out a false match on the name.) AutoGen's `SelectorGroupChatManager` (`_selector_group_chat.py`, microsoft/autogen) selects the next speaker with a ChatCompletion model call inside the manager itself — a 1:N inference in an actor that neither acts on nor answers for a misroute, the exact fallthrough hazard `work_model.md#pull-is-the-only-delivery-assignment-constrains-eligibility` names. None of the three frameworks has a claim/lease primitive anywhere in this path: no persisted lease with a holder read back after the write (`work_model.md#the-claim-and-the-lease-are-one-primitive`), no `assigned_to`-as-eligibility distinct from a holder (`work_model.md#assignment-restricts-eligibility-it-never-creates-a-lease`), and no analogue of an `unspawnable_assignee` checkpoint for a routing decision that resolves to nobody accountable. This is a genuinely different failure mode from the one dropped, not the same one restated: "sequencing agents in a run" is a coordination-convenience claim these frameworks answer directly; "work is pushed by a router/manager/scheduler that cannot be held accountable for a misroute, versus claimed by the principal that answers for the outcome" is an accountability claim none of them make any provision for. It is also not redundant with the two modes that already SURVIVE: identity collapse is about whether an executed action is attributable to a distinct signed principal after the fact, and advisory-only governance is about whether a declared gate mechanically binds — neither is about how the executor for a step gets selected in the first place. Restated failure mode, replacing the dropped one: "the framework's own scheduler, crew, or manager selects and pushes the next executor by topology, delegation, or model inference, with no claim a principal makes for itself and no lease an executor holds that the dispatcher must read back — so a wrong selection reaches an executor with nobody accountable for the choice." What Ateles resolves against it (`work_model.md#pull-is-the-only-delivery-assignment-constrains-eligibility` through `#the-claim-and-the-lease-are-one-primitive`): work reaches an agent only by its own claim, `assigned_to` narrows eligibility without ever installing a holder, and the claim and the lease are one primitive whose holder is read back after the write — so exclusivity and accountability are the same fact, not two.

- IDENTITY COLLAPSE — SURVIVES, unchanged from the prior test, and reinforced by the same kind-of-state gap above: neither framework's Item/MemoryRecord has a field for "which principal authorized this under what scope" — `source` on a CrewAI record is an origin tag on a text blob, not a signed, distinct, per-agent identity backing a typed action. None of the three frameworks model authority, accountability, or per-agent signed identity distinct from execution; they coordinate computation, not legitimate action.

- INSTRUCTIONS AS GOVERNANCE (advisory-only) — SURVIVES, unchanged. None of the three frameworks offer mechanically-binding gates; tool-allowlists and prompts in all of them are advisory in-code, enforced (if at all) by a separate sandbox/data layer the frameworks themselves do not provide.

CANDIDATES ELIMINATED, RESTATED, OR DEMOTED ACROSS BOTH RE-RUNS: manual sequencing, initially dropped outright as framing the competitor's own category, is on further operator-directed test (push vs. pull, third pass) RESTATED rather than dropped — see above; the coordination-convenience version of the claim is correctly conceded to the frameworks, but a distinct accountability claim about how the executor is selected survives under primary-source evidence none of the three frameworks answer. Zero-context restarts and no standing memory are restated with kind-of-state (typed/attributable/correctable record vs. untyped execution/recall state) as the primary discriminator and process/horizon as its downstream consequence — at the literal original wording a shipping framework could otherwise claim a persistence feature exists, which is why kind-of-state rather than mere reach is the correct test. Identity collapse and advisory-only governance are unchanged and remain failure modes that survive without restatement from the second pass, and identity collapse is reinforced by the same evidence; the push/pull restatement of manual sequencing is a distinct fourth surviving mode, not a restatement of either.
